misconceptions: Any service can be scaled horizontally without changes

templates.question: What is the difference between vertical and horizontal scaling, and what does an application need in order to scale horizontally?
keyPoints: Vertical scaling uses a bigger machine: simple, but limited and a single point of failure
Horizontal scaling adds machines behind a load balancer, adding capacity and redundancy
Application instances must be stateless: sessions in a shared store or in tokens
The data layer must cope too; the database is often the next bottleneck

templates.question: How does a load balancer distribute traffic, and how does it know that a server is unhealthy?
keyPoints: Algorithms such as round robin, least connections, or hashing on a key
Layer 4 balancers route TCP connections; layer 7 balancers understand HTTP and can route by path and terminate TLS
Health checks take failing instances out of rotation
Sticky sessions make scaling and failover harder

templates.question: A web app keeps each user's shopping cart in the HTTP session in server memory. After a second instance is added behind a load balancer, users start losing their carts. Why, and how do you fix it?
keyPoints: Each instance has its own memory, and requests of one user land on different instances
Sticky sessions hide the problem but lose carts when an instance fails
Move the state out of the instances: a shared session store (for example Redis with Spring Session) or the database
Stateless instances are interchangeable, so they can be added and replaced freely

templates.question: Estimate the storage and the requests per second for a service that stores 10 million new 1 KB records per day and serves 100 reads for every write.
keyPoints: 10 million times 1 KB is about 10 GB a day, roughly 3.7 TB a year before replication and indexes
About 10 million / 86,400 = 116 writes per second on average
About 11,600 reads per second on average
Peaks are several times the average, so plan for them
The numbers drive decisions such as caching reads and partitioning storage

templates.question: After two more application servers were added, throughput barely improved and latency went up. What would you investigate?
keyPoints: A shared bottleneck behind the application servers: database CPU, locks or connections
Connection pools: instances times pool size may exceed the database's connection limit
A downstream dependency or cache that is saturated
Uneven load distribution, for example from sticky sessions
Measure each tier's utilisation to find the saturated resource

misconceptions: A cache can be treated as the source of truth
A longer TTL is always better
Caching a slow query has no downside

templates.question: Explain cache-aside, write-through and write-behind caching. Which would you use for a product catalogue?
keyPoints: Cache-aside: read the cache, on a miss load from the database and fill the cache; writes go to the database and invalidate the key
Write-through: every write updates the cache and the database synchronously
Write-behind: the cache acknowledges and writes to the database later, with a risk of losing writes
A read-heavy catalogue suits cache-aside with a TTL and invalidation on update

templates.question: Why is cache invalidation hard, and how do you keep a cache reasonably consistent with the database?
keyPoints: Copies of the data live in caches while the database changes, often in several places
Invalidate or update the cached entry on every write, after the database commit
A TTL bounds how stale an entry can get when an invalidation is missed
A race: a reader can put a stale value back between the write and the invalidation
Decide per kind of data how much staleness is acceptable

templates.question: Every hour, when a popular cache entry expires, database CPU spikes and requests time out. What is happening, and how do you prevent it?
keyPoints: A cache stampede: many concurrent misses all hit the database at once
Let one request recompute the value while others wait or get the old value (request coalescing, a lock)
Serve the stale value while refreshing it, or refresh before expiry
Add jitter to TTLs so that keys do not expire together

templates.question: Where would you cache in a system with a browser client, a CDN, an API service and a database, and what would you cache at each layer?
keyPoints: Browser: HTTP caching with Cache-Control and ETags
CDN: static assets and public responses, close to users
In-process cache: small, hot, rarely changing data, separate per instance
Distributed cache such as Redis: data shared between instances
Database: its own buffer cache, and precomputed results such as materialised views

misconceptions: Read replicas always return the latest data
CAP means always choosing two of three properties
Sharding is the first fix for a slow database

templates.question: What are leader-follower replication and read replicas used for, and what is replication lag?
keyPoints: Writes go to the leader, which streams its changes to the followers
Read replicas scale reads and are candidates for failover
With asynchronous replication followers lag behind, so their reads can be stale
Read-your-writes: send a user's reads to the leader for a while after they write
Synchronous replication avoids data loss at the cost of write latency

templates.question: How would you shard a table of user data across several databases, and what becomes harder after sharding?
keyPoints: Choose a shard key that spreads the data evenly and that most queries include, such as the user id
Hash partitioning spreads load; range partitioning keeps ranges together but risks hot spots
Consistent hashing or a lookup directory eases rebalancing
Queries, joins and transactions across shards become hard
Resharding is costly, so it is not the first fix for a slow database

templates.question: What does the CAP theorem actually say, and how does it show up when you choose a database?
keyPoints: During a network partition a distributed system must choose between consistency and availability
Without a partition both are possible; the everyday trade-off is between latency and consistency (PACELC)
A consistent system refuses or delays requests during a partition
An available system answers with possibly stale data and reconciles later
The right choice depends on the data: payments versus a social feed

templates.question: Users update their profile and see the old values when the page reloads, but a few seconds later the new values appear. What is the likely cause?
keyPoints: Reads are served by an asynchronous read replica that lags behind the leader
The user does not read their own write
Route a user's reads to the leader for a short time after a write, or wait until the replica has caught up
Monitor replication lag

misconceptions: Brokers deliver every message exactly once by default
Kafka keeps messages ordered across the whole topic
Publishing an event after the database commit in the same method is atomic

templates.question: What is the difference between a message queue such as RabbitMQ and a log such as Kafka, and when would you use each?
keyPoints: A queue delivers each message to one consumer and removes it once it is acknowledged; it suits distributing tasks
A log appends messages durably, and each consumer group keeps its own position (offset)
A log can be replayed and read by many independent consumer groups
Kafka keeps order within a partition and scales by adding partitions
Logs suit event streams and replay; queues suit work queues and flexible routing

templates.question: Most brokers deliver at least once. What does that mean for consumers, and how do you make processing idempotent?
keyPoints: A message can be delivered more than once, for example after a timeout or a crash before the acknowledgement
Consumers must handle duplicates
Record the processed message ids (with a unique constraint) in the same transaction as the effect
Or make the operation naturally idempotent: an upsert, or setting a state rather than adding to it
Exactly-once processing needs the effect and the deduplication to be atomic

templates.question: When an order is saved, an OrderCreated event must be published to Kafka. Sometimes the order is saved but the event is never published. How would you fix that?
keyPoints: The database commit and the publish are two separate writes that cannot be made atomic (the dual-write problem)
Write the event to an outbox table in the same database transaction as the order
A relay (a poller, or change data capture such as Debezium) publishes the outbox rows and marks them sent
Delivery becomes at least once, so consumers must deduplicate

templates.question: A consumer group's lag keeps growing during peak hours, and a few messages fail repeatedly and block their partition. What would you do?
keyPoints: Measure the processing time and throughput per consumer
Add consumers up to the number of partitions, and more partitions if needed
Speed up processing: batching, fewer or faster downstream calls
Retry a failing message a few times with backoff, then move it to a dead-letter topic so the partition keeps moving
Alert on lag

templates.question: How do you keep the events of the same order in sequence when Kafka has several partitions and consumers?
keyPoints: Kafka guarantees order only within a partition
Use the order id as the message key so that all its events go to the same partition
One consumer of a group reads a partition, in order
Retries or parallel processing inside a consumer can still reorder events
Version numbers let a consumer ignore events older than what it has applied

misconceptions: Offset pagination works well at any size
A POST request can be retried safely without extra measures

templates.question: How would you implement rate limiting for a public API? Compare the token bucket and the fixed window approaches.
keyPoints: A fixed window counts requests per interval; it is simple but allows bursts at the window boundaries
Sliding windows smooth those boundaries
A token bucket refills tokens at a steady rate up to a capacity and allows bounded bursts
With several instances the counters need a shared store (for example Redis with atomic operations), or limits per instance
A rejected request gets 429 Too Many Requests with Retry-After

templates.question: Compare offset and cursor (keyset) pagination. Which would you use for an infinite-scroll feed?
keyPoints: Offset and limit are simple and allow jumping to a page
With offset the database still reads and discards the skipped rows, so deep pages are slow, and pages shift when rows are inserted
Cursor pagination continues after the last seen sort key (WHERE id < ? ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT n) using an index
It stays fast and stable under inserts but cannot jump to page N
An infinite-scroll feed suits a cursor

templates.question: A mobile client retries a payment request after a timeout, and the customer is charged twice. How would you design the API to prevent that?
keyPoints: The client sends an Idempotency-Key header that is unique per payment and reuses it when retrying
The server stores the key with the result and returns the stored result for a repeat
A unique constraint or lock handles two concurrent requests with the same key
Keys expire after a retention period

templates.question: After a release that renamed a JSON field, older versions of the mobile app start failing. How should the API change have been made?
keyPoints: Renaming or removing a field is a breaking change
Change additively: add the new field, keep the old one and deprecate it
Clients should ignore fields they do not know
Breaking changes need a new API version, with both versions running during the migration
Contract tests catch breaking changes before release

misconceptions: Retrying immediately and without limit improves reliability
Logs alone are enough to debug a distributed system

templates.question: Why does every remote call need a timeout, and how should retries be done so that they do not make an outage worse?
keyPoints: Without a timeout a slow dependency holds threads and connections until the caller fails as well (cascading failure)
Retry only transient failures, and only idempotent operations
Use exponential backoff with jitter and a limit on attempts
Retry at one layer only, within a budget
Propagate deadlines so inner calls do not outlive their caller

templates.question: How does a circuit breaker work, and what problem does it solve?
keyPoints: It counts failures of calls to a dependency
Past a threshold it opens, and calls fail fast instead of waiting
After a cool-down it lets a few trial calls through (half-open) and closes again if they succeed
It protects the caller's resources and gives the dependency time to recover
It is usually combined with a fallback

templates.question: How would you define SLOs for a checkout API, and how would you use its error budget?
keyPoints: Indicators of what users experience: the share of successful requests and latency percentiles such as p99
An SLO is a target over a window, for example 99.9% successful requests over 30 days
The error budget is the rest: at 99.9% about 43 minutes of failure a month
Spend the budget on releases and experiments; when it runs out, prioritise reliability work
Alert on how fast the budget burns

templates.question: A request that passes through five services is sometimes slow, but each service's own metrics look normal. How would you find where the time goes?
keyPoints: Distributed tracing (for example OpenTelemetry) with a trace id passed along every call
The spans show the time spent in each service and call, including waiting and retries
Logs carrying the trace id can be correlated across services
Look at tail latency (p99), not averages
Typical causes: retries, waiting for the slowest of several parallel calls, waiting for a pool
